lines.text: Chapter one. From a desert bet to an empire.
lines.say: Chapter one. From a desert bet to an empire.

lines.text: On March 19, 1931, in the middle of the Great Depression, Nevada legalized wide-open gambling.
lines.say: On March nineteenth, nineteen thirty-one, in the middle of the Great Depression, Nevada legalized wide-open gambling.

lines.text: The state needed money, and a casino tax looked a lot easier than mining.
lines.say: The state needed money, and legal casinos meant license fees and taxes flowing in.

lines.text: By 1955, the state created the Nevada Gaming Control Board to license and watch the industry.
lines.say: By nineteen fifty-five, the state had created the Nevada Gaming Control Board to license and watch the whole industry.

lines.text: That board still counts every dollar casinos win, month by month. Most of our numbers today come from it.
lines.say: That board still counts every dollar casinos win, month by month, and most of the numbers in this video come from it.

lines.say: Then it roared back to a new record in twenty twenty-one, and it's set another record every single year since.

lines.text: That total includes about $51 billion from traditional casino games in 2025.
lines.say: That total includes about fifty-one billion dollars from traditional casino games like slots and tables.

lines.text: And states collected about $18 billion in gaming taxes on top of it.
lines.say: And states collected about eighteen billion dollars in gaming taxes from all of it.

lines.text: So how does a business win that reliably? It starts with one tiny number.
lines.say: So how does a business win that reliably, year after year? It all starts with one tiny number.

lines.text: Chapter two. The edge.
lines.say: Chapter two. The edge.

lines.text: The house edge is the slice of every bet the casino expects to keep over the long run.
lines.say: The house edge is the slice of every bet that the casino expects to keep over the long run.

lines.text: It's not a fee you see. It's hidden in the payouts, which are always a little smaller than the true odds.
lines.say: It's not a fee you ever see. It's hidden inside the payouts, which are always a little smaller than the true odds.

lines.text: Roulette shows it perfectly. An American wheel has 38 pockets: 1 to 36, plus 0 and 00.
lines.say: Roulette shows it perfectly. An American wheel has thirty-eight pockets: the numbers one to thirty-six, plus a zero and a double zero.

lines.text: So your number hits 1 time in 38. Fair pay would be 37 to 1. The casino pays 35 to 1.
lines.say: So your number hits one time in thirty-eight. A fair payout would be thirty-seven to one. The casino pays thirty-five to one.

lines.text: Let's do the math. Put $1 on every number: that's $38 on the table.
lines.say: Let's do the math. Put one dollar on every single number. That's thirty-eight dollars on the table.

lines.text: One number must win. You get $35 in winnings plus your $1 back: $36.
lines.say: One number has to win. You get thirty-five dollars in winnings, plus your one dollar back. That's thirty-six dollars.

lines.text: You bet $38 and got back $36. You lost $2, every single spin, no matter what.
lines.say: You bet thirty-eight dollars and got back thirty-six. You lost two dollars on that spin, no matter which number came up.

lines.text: $2 divided by $38 is 5.26%. That's the house edge on American roulette.
lines.say: Two dollars divided by thirty-eight is about five point three percent. That's the house edge on American roulette.

lines.text: Take away the double zero and the edge drops to 2.70%. One extra pocket nearly doubles it.
lines.say: Take away the double zero, like a European wheel, and the edge drops to about two point seven percent. One extra pocket nearly doubles it.

lines.text: Five cents on a dollar sounds small. Anyone can win a spin, a night, even a lucky weekend.
lines.say: About five cents on a dollar sounds tiny. And anyone can win a spin, a night, even a lucky weekend.

lines.text: But the casino isn't playing one spin. It's playing millions of them.
lines.say: But the casino isn't playing one spin. It's playing millions of them, all day, every day.

lines.text: That's the law of large numbers: the more bets, the closer results get to the math.
lines.say: That's the law of large numbers. The more bets there are, the closer the results get to the math.

lines.text: For you, the edge is a small tilt. For the casino, it's closer to a salary.
lines.say: For you, the edge is a small tilt you barely feel. For the casino, it's a lot closer to a salary.

lines.text: Every game has its own version of the edge, and some are sneakier than roulette.
lines.say: Every game has its own version of the edge, and some of them are a lot sneakier than roulette.

lines.text: Blackjack is famous as the player-friendly game. But watch one tiny rule.
lines.say: Blackjack is famous as the player-friendly game. But watch what happens with one tiny rule.

lines.text: A natural blackjack traditionally pays 3 to 2. On a $10 bet, that's $15.
lines.say: A natural blackjack traditionally pays three to two. On a ten-dollar bet, that's fifteen dollars.

lines.text: Many tables now pay 6 to 5 instead. Same cards, same bet, just $12.
lines.say: Many tables now pay six to five instead. Same cards, same bet, but you only get twelve dollars.

lines.text: You get a blackjack only about 4.75% of hands, so it feels harmless.
lines.say: You only get a blackjack about four point seven five percent of the time, so the change feels harmless.

lines.text: But that one change adds about 1.39 percentage points to the house edge.
lines.say: But that one change adds about one point four percentage points to the house edge.

lines.text: Baccarat, the high-roller favorite, uses a different trick: a commission.
lines.say: Baccarat, the high-roller favorite, uses a different trick. It charges a commission.

lines.text: The banker hand wins a bit more often, so the casino takes 5% of every banker win.
lines.say: The banker hand wins a little more often than the player hand, so the casino takes five percent of every banker win.

lines.text: That leaves a 1.06% edge on banker, 1.24% on player, and a painful 14.36% on a tie bet.
lines.say: That leaves the house just over one percent on banker, about one point two on player, and a painful fourteen point four percent on a tie.

lines.text: Then there are slots, which bring in more than two-thirds of Nevada's gaming win.
lines.say: And then there are slot machines, which bring in more than two-thirds of Nevada's gaming win.

lines.text: In August 2026 alone, Nevada slots won $944.7 million.
lines.say: In August twenty twenty-six alone, Nevada's slot machines won about nine hundred forty-five million dollars.

lines.text: A slot's edge is set by its software. Nevada only requires machines to pay back at least 75%.
lines.say: A slot's edge is set inside its software. And Nevada only requires each machine to pay back at least seventy-five percent over time.

lines.text: Most pay back far more than that. The share the casino keeps is called the hold.
lines.say: Most machines pay back far more than that. The share the casino actually keeps is called the hold.

lines.text: Across Nevada, slots held about 7.1% of the money played in 2025, and a UNLV study found machines have gotten tighter over the past decade.
lines.say: Across Nevada, slots held about seven point one percent of the money played in twenty twenty-five, and a UNLV study found the machines have gotten tighter over the past decade.

lines.text: UNLV researchers put it simply.
lines.say: Researchers at UNLV put it simply: hold percentage, the portion of money gambled that the casino retains, has a huge impact on casino revenues.

lines.text: State regulators have said any tightening stays within legal limits. It just means players win a little less on average.
lines.say: State regulators have said any tightening stays within legal limits. It simply means players win a little less, on average, than they used to.

lines.text: Chapter three. How small edges get big.
lines.say: Chapter three. How small edges get big.

lines.text: Here's the fact that surprises people: the edge hits every dollar you bet, not the dollars you bring.
lines.say: Here's the fact that surprises people most. The edge hits every dollar you bet, not the dollars you walk in with.

lines.text: Say you sit at a slot with $100 and bet $1 a spin.
lines.say: Say you sit down at a slot machine with one hundred dollars and bet one dollar a spin.

lines.text: You win some, you lose some, and you keep feeding the wins back in. After 1,000 spins, you've wagered $1,000.
lines.say: You win some, you lose some, and you keep feeding the wins back in. After a thousand spins, you've wagered one thousand dollars.

lines.text: At Nevada's 2025 average hold of 7.1%, the average loss is 7.1% of $1,000: $71.
lines.say: At Nevada's twenty twenty-five average hold of seven point one percent, the average loss is seven point one percent of a thousand dollars. That's seventy-one dollars.

lines.text: You brought $100 and, on average, you walk out with $29. A 7.1% edge ate 71% of your money.
lines.say: You brought one hundred dollars, and on average you walk out with twenty-nine. An edge of about seven percent ate seventy-one percent of your money.

lines.text: The casino word for this is churn: the same dollars get bet again and again.
lines.say: The industry word for this is churn. The same dollars get bet again, and again, and again.

lines.text: Now scale it up. MGM Resorts runs some of the biggest casinos on the Strip.
lines.say: Now let's scale it up. MGM Resorts runs some of the biggest casinos on the Las Vegas Strip.

lines.text: In 2025, gamblers put $24.6 billion through its Las Vegas slot machines.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five, gamblers put about twenty-four point six billion dollars through its Las Vegas slot machines.

lines.text: MGM kept $2.3 billion of it, a win rate of 9.4%.
lines.say: MGM kept about two point three billion dollars of it. That's a win rate of about nine point four percent.

lines.text: Tables look even stranger. MGM's Strip tables won 25.2% of the drop in 2025.
lines.say: Table games look even stranger. MGM's Strip tables won about twenty-five percent of the drop in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: That's not because the edge is 25%. The drop is only the cash swapped for chips.
lines.say: That's not because the edge is twenty-five percent. The drop is only the cash people swap for chips.

lines.text: Those chips get bet over and over. Churn turns a small edge into a quarter of the cash.
lines.say: Those chips get bet over and over. That's churn again, turning a small edge into a quarter of the cash.

lines.text: So time and speed are the real price. Faster games and longer sessions mean more bets for the edge to work on.
lines.say: So time and speed are the real price. Faster games and longer sessions mean more bets for the edge to work on.

lines.text: Chapter four. The hotel is the business.
lines.say: Chapter four. The hotel is the business.

lines.text: Remember the surprise from the start? Here are the full numbers.
lines.say: Remember that surprise from the start? Here are the full numbers.

lines.text: In the state's fiscal year ending June 2025, 51 big Strip casinos brought in $21.1 billion in total revenue.
lines.say: In the state's fiscal year ending June twenty twenty-five, fifty-one big Strip casinos brought in twenty-one point one billion dollars in total revenue.

lines.say: Gaming was only about twenty-six percent of it. Hotel rooms alone brought in seven point one billion dollars.

lines.text: Rooms beat gambling. Add food, shows, shops and nightlife, and the rest is nearly three-quarters of revenue.
lines.say: Rooms beat gambling. Add in the food, shows, shops and nightlife, and non-gaming makes up nearly three-quarters of revenue.

lines.text: The average Strip room went for about $251 a night, and occupancy was about 89%.
lines.say: The average Strip room went for about two hundred fifty-one dollars a night, and the hotels were about eighty-nine percent full.

lines.text: So why keep the casino at all? Because the floor feeds everything else, and everything else feeds the floor.
lines.say: So why keep the casino at all? Because the floor feeds everything else, and everything else feeds the floor.

lines.text: That's what comps are. Free rooms and meals are funded by what the casino expects you to lose.
lines.say: That's what comps really are. The free rooms and meals are paid for out of what the casino expects you to lose.

lines.text: Casinos call it theoretical loss: how much you bet, times the house edge. They give a slice back to keep you coming.
lines.say: Casinos call it theoretical loss: how much you bet, times the house edge. They hand a slice of it back to keep you coming.

lines.text: It's a clever loop. The same guest pays for the room, the dinner, and the edge.
lines.say: It's a clever loop. The same guest pays for the room, the dinner, and the edge.

lines.text: Chapter five. Where the house can lose.
lines.say: Chapter five. Where the house can lose.

lines.text: If the math always wins, is running a casino easy money? Not quite.
lines.say: So if the math always wins, is running a casino easy money? Not quite.

lines.text: Risk one: variance. The edge is certain over millions of bets, not over one month.
lines.say: Risk one is variance. The edge is certain over millions of bets, but not over a single month.

lines.text: Luck cuts both ways for the house. MGM's Strip tables won 24.4% of the drop in 2024 and 25.2% in 2025.
lines.say: Luck cuts both ways for the house. MGM's Strip tables won about twenty-four percent of the drop in twenty twenty-four, and about twenty-five percent in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: That 0.8-point swing on $6.13 billion of drop is about $49 million. A cold streak can move it the other way just as fast.

lines.text: Risk two: fewer visitors. Las Vegas drew 38.5 million people in 2025, 7.5% fewer than in 2024.

lines.say: Risk three is costs. Giant resorts come with giant debts.

lines.text: People can now bet from the couch, and that money doesn't pay for a hotel room.

post.tiktok: A 7.1% slot hold can eat $71 of a $100 bankroll. Here's how churn works.
post.yt_desc:
Nevada casinos won nearly $15.8 billion from gamblers in 2025, a fifth straight record, even as Las Vegas had 7.5% fewer visitors. This video breaks down how casinos are built to win: the house edge hidden in every payout (with the roulette math), 6-to-5 blackjack, baccarat's commission, slot hold, and how churn turns a small edge into big money, using MGM Resorts' 2025 10-K. It also shows the surprise that hotel rooms now out-earn gambling on the Las Vegas Strip, and where the house can still lose.
